title: Edge reconstruction conjecture
formal: For every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H with at least four edges, does equality of their edge decks \(D_{E}(G)=D_{E}(H)\) imply \(G\cong H\)?
why: A longstanding reconstruction principle that tests how much global graph structure survives individual edge losses.

progress.text: Harary poses the edge reconstruction conjecture, as recounted by Calle and Gould.
An algebraic reformulation preserves the open ordinary conjecture while a pooled-deck generalization is disproved.
A preprint addresses selected-card reconstruction within the known class of maximal planar graphs.

references.title: Wikipedia: Reconstruction conjecture
references.locator: Discovery source; retrieved 2026-09-11. Evidence locator: Edge Reconstruction Conjecture

definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and parallel edges are excluded. Isolated vertices and disconnected graphs are allowed. For \(e\in E\), let \(G- e=(V,E\setminus \{e\})\): deleting an edge retains every vertex, including vertices that become isolated. Two graphs are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. Write \([G- e]\) for the isomorphism class with vertex labels forgotten. The edge deck is the multiset \(D_{E}(G)=\{[G- e]:e\in E\}\); each edge contributes one entry, so repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. Deck equality requires each isomorphism class to occur equally often. Entries have no common vertex labeling and do not identify the deleted edge. The question concerns uniqueness from a deck known to arise from a graph, with no efficiency requirement on reconstruction.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all finite simple graphs with at least four edges, or give two nonisomorphic such graphs and prove that their complete edge decks agree with multiplicities. A result for a bounded number of vertices, a promised graph class or decks pooled from multiple graphs does not settle the universal claim.

context_blocks.title: What information survives
context_blocks.text: Think of making one copy of a network for each connection and deleting a different connection from each copy. The copies are shuffled and their vertex names erased. The conjecture says their shapes and repetition counts still identify the original network. For a four-cycle, the deck consists of four copies of the path on four vertices.

context_blocks.title: Why at least four edges
context_blocks.text: The threshold excludes a real ambiguity. A triangle together with one isolated vertex and the three-leaf star are nonisomorphic four-vertex graphs with three edges. Deleting any edge from either leaves a three-vertex path together with an isolated vertex. Their edge decks therefore agree, each containing three copies of the same graph.

context_blocks.title: Edge and vertex deletion
context_blocks.text: An edge-deleted graph has the original number of vertices. A vertex-deleted graph loses a vertex and all edges incident to it. The imported McKay reference primarily studies the latter and its set-deck variant. Calle and Gould give the precise edge-deck formulation used here; retaining multiplicities and isolated vertices is part of that model.

context_blocks.title: Recent work and the remaining target
context_blocks.text: The 2025 K-theory paper reformulates the ordinary conjecture and disproves a stronger statement about recovering several graphs from their pooled decks; it explicitly does not settle the single-graph conjecture. A September 2026 preprint instead studies how few selected entries suffice when the original graph is promised to be maximal planar. Such additional information changes the reconstruction task.

sentences: Delete each edge of a graph in turn, erase vertex labels and collect the resulting graphs with repetitions.
The edge reconstruction conjecture asks whether this multiset determines every finite simple graph with at least four edges.
All vertices survive deletion, and repeated copies of the same graph remain significant.
A triangle plus an isolated vertex and a three-leaf star show why a three-edge version fails.
Recent algebraic reformulations and results for promised graph classes leave the general uniqueness question open.
